ch08.anchor: fallen from it now, it sweeps beneath the tree
ch08.note: The lampoons pun on the defector’s court title, Hōki-no-kami, “Governor of Hōki,” which sounds like hōki, a broom—hence the “old broom.” And “beneath the tree” renders ki no shita, which is also Kinoshita, Hideyoshi’s original surname before he took the names Hashiba and Toyotomi. The cast-off broom of Ieyasu’s house now sweeps in Kinoshita’s—that is, in Hideyoshi’s—service. (Printed folio 462.)

Asahi-hime (1543–1590), Hideyoshi’s half-sister, was married off to Ieyasu in 1586 to bind the two houses, her existing husband forced aside. To coax the wary Ieyasu up to the capital to make his formal submission, Hideyoshi went further still and sent his own aged mother, the Ōmandokoro (the honorific title of the mother of a regent), to Ieyasu as a hostage. The whole maneuver is historical. (Printed folio 463.)

Gaspar Coelho (c.1530–1590) was Vice-Provincial, the head of the Jesuit mission in Japan. The ranks of his party descend from padre, an ordained priest, through irmão, a lay brother, to dōjuku, a Japanese lay catechist and helper, and the boys of the seminary. This audience with Hideyoshi in 1586, reported here from Frois’s letter, came only a year before Hideyoshi abruptly turned on the mission. (Printed folio 464.)

Hideyoshi’s celebrated portable tea room, its walls, ceiling, pillars and utensils all sheathed in gold and built to be taken apart and carried. He had it set up at the imperial court in 1586, and again at Nagoya during the Korean war. To his admirers it was a wonder; to his critics, then and now, the very emblem of his gaudy excess. (Printed folio 466.)

ch08.anchor: proclaimed the ban on the Kirishitan
ch08.note: Hideyoshi’s expulsion edict of 1587, the Bateren-tsuihōrei, ordering the missionaries out of Japan within twenty days while leaving the profitable Portuguese trade untouched. Enforcement was fitful at first and the mission survived underground; but the edict opened the long persecution that would end, under the Tokugawa, in the near-total suppression of Christianity in Japan. (Printed folio 468.)

ch08.anchor: Maeda Tokuun, called also Seyakuin Zensō
ch08.note: Seyakuin Zensō (1526–1599), a former Tendai monk of Mount Hiei who became Hideyoshi’s physician and a man of great influence at his court. The Jesuit reports, hostile witnesses, cast him as the procurer of women for the Taikō and a grave enemy of the mission; the lurid portrait here is drawn from them, and is best read as their view rather than plain fact. (Printed folio 468.)

The Jurakudai, the “Mansion of Assembled Pleasures,” the sumptuous palace-fortress Hideyoshi raised in Kyoto in 1587 as the seat of his regency, and where he received the Emperor in state the next year. He handed it on to his heir Hidetsugu; and when he destroyed Hidetsugu in 1595 he had the whole palace pulled down, so that scarcely a trace of it remains. (Printed folio 462.)

ch08.anchor: the land of the Chollima, the Thousand-League Horse
ch08.note: The Chōllima, the “thousand-li horse” of East Asian legend, that could gallop a thousand leagues in a day. The author, a lifelong man of the left writing in 1964, reaches for the name pointedly: it is also that of the Chollima Movement, the mass labor-mobilization campaign of North Korea in exactly those years. His warmth toward “the land of the Chollima,” set against a monument urging Japan to relearn Hideyoshi’s appetite for the continent, is of a piece with the anti-militarist stance he takes throughout. (Printed folio 492.)

ch08.anchor: took to calling him Sute, the Cast-off
ch08.note: By a widespread folk belief, a child formally “thrown away” and picked up again—or merely given a throwaway name such as Sute, “Cast-off,” or Hiroi, “Foundling”—would cheat the ill luck that carried off so many infants, and grow up strong. Hideyoshi, who had lost children young, named both his sons this way. It availed neither: Tsurumatsu died at two, and Hideyori at the fall of Ōsaka. (Printed folio 484.)

ch08.anchor: This Hiroi was the later Hideyori
ch08.note: Toyotomi Hideyori (1593–1615), Hideyoshi’s son and heir by the Lady Yodo. After Hideyoshi’s death in 1598 real power passed to Ieyasu, who won the realm at Sekigahara in 1600 and took the title of shogun. Hideyori was penned up in Ōsaka castle; and in 1615 Ieyasu stormed and burned it, and Hideyori and his mother killed themselves in the flames. It is that last act of the saga the author says he means to tell in the sequel. (Printed folio 496.)

ch08.anchor: Odawara castle too opened its gates
ch08.note: The siege of Odawara in 1590 destroyed the Later Hōjō, the last great house holding out against Hideyoshi, and completed his unification of Japan. Its consequence for this story is Ieyasu’s reward: he was moved out of his ancestral provinces into the newly conquered Kantō, and made his seat at a small, half-ruined castle town called Edo—the future Tokyo. (Printed folio 486.)

The name survives to this day. Hanzōmon, the “Hanzō Gate” on the western side of the Imperial Palace—the former Edo castle—in Tokyo, and the subway line named for it, still carry the name of Hattori Hanzō, whose Iga men were quartered just outside it to guard the castle’s landward rear. (Printed folio 488.)

Hideyoshi’s two invasions of Korea, of 1592 and 1597, named in Japan for the era-names Bunroku and Keichō, and in Korea the Imjin and Jeongyu wars. Launched to feed his boundless ambition and to open a road into Ming China beyond, they laid waste much of the peninsula, won nothing lasting, and were broken off at his death in 1598. The Korean and Chinese names, and the author’s flat verdict of a “war of aggression,” are given here as he wrote them. (Printed folio 494.)

Yi Sun-sin (1545–1598), admiral of the Korean navy and his country’s foremost national hero, who broke Japanese command of the sea in a run of victories and severed the invaders’ supply lines. He is famed for the armored “turtle-ships” (geobukseon) described here, low vessels roofed over against boarders. He fell in the war’s last battle, in 1598. (Printed folio 498.)

ch08.anchor: This corridor is a nightingale floor
ch08.note: An uguisubari, or “nightingale floor,” is a floor built on purpose so that its boards chirp underfoot, their nails working against iron clamps, to betray an intruder’s tread. Real examples survive, the most famous at Nijō castle in Kyoto. Here the device is turned against Goemon by a castle Hanzō’s ninja helped design for the very purpose of trapping him. (Printed folio 516.)

ch08.anchor: This plover incense-burner was a famed vessel
ch08.note: The chidori no kōro, or “plover incense-burner,” belongs to the popular legend of Goemon’s capture: creeping to the sleeping Hideyoshi’s pillow, he is betrayed when the burner cries out like a plover. The motif runs through the kabuki and puppet plays. The author gives it as one of the “surface” fictions grown up around the historical execution, and sets against it his own reading of Goemon as an avenger of the peasants. (Printed folio 521.)

The earliest record, and a genuine one—though the author’s attribution slips. He credits Yamashina Tokitsugu, who died in 1579; the entry he quotes, under the twenty-fourth of the eighth month of Bunroku 3, is in fact from the diary of Tokitsugu’s son Tokitsune, the Tokitsune-kyō ki. It records a thief and his fellows boiled in a cauldron at the Sanjō riverbed, but gives no name. The name “Ishikawa Goemon” is first fixed to the event only in 1642, by Hayashi Razan’s Toyotomi Hideyoshi-fu; all the rest is legend grown up around a bare and brutal fact. (Printed folio 522.)
